quote.exact: τ = k·i (torque constant k, N·m/A) V = R·i + k·ω (winding resistance R, speed ω)
quote.suffix: Eliminate the current and the m

comments.author: elliot
comments.body: Could you go into more detail please

comments.author: Codex
comments.body:
Those equations describe **two linked effects: current creates torque, and rotation generates a voltage that reduces the current.** The straight line describes their steady balance at a fixed supply voltage.

**1. Current creates torque: `τ = kₜ i`.**

The winding carries current through the motor’s magnetic field, producing a twisting force. Here, `τ` is motor torque in N·m, `i` is current in amperes, and `kₜ = 0.012 N·m/A`: each ampere produces 0.012 N·m of torque. Doubling current doubles torque in this model.

**2. Rotation creates back-EMF: `V = Ri + kₑω`.**

A spinning motor also acts as a generator. Its generated voltage, `e = kₑω`, opposes the applied voltage. The voltage left to drive current through the winding resistance is therefore `V − e`:

```text
i = (V − kₑω)/R
```

Here, `ω` is shaft speed relative to the case, in rad/s. The lesson fixes the case to the mount and connects the shaft to the rotor inertia and load. Its electrical terminals connect across the 12 V supply. See [system connections](/Users/elliot/physics-simulator/lessons/motor-torque-speed/motor.system.json:240).

The lesson writes both constants as `k` because they have equal numerical values in consistent SI units for this ideal motor. Their units differ: `kₜ` is N·m/A, while `kₑ` is V·s/rad. This equality makes converted electrical power `ei` equal mechanical power `τω`.

**Combining the equations gives the line.**

```text
τ = kₜ(V − kₑω)/R
  = 0.072 − 0.000072ω   N·m
```

Using the lesson’s authored values, the calculated steady operating points are:

| Opposing load | Current | Back-EMF | Speed |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 N·m | 0 A | 12 V | 1000 rad/s |
| 0.02 N·m | 1.67 A | 8.67 V | 722 rad/s |
| 0.04 N·m | 3.33 A | 5.33 V | 444 rad/s |
| 0.072 N·m, stall | 6 A | 0 V | 0 rad/s |

For example, at 0.02 N·m, torque balance requires `i = 0.02/0.012 = 1.67 A`. Resistance uses `Ri = 3.33 V`, leaving 8.67 V of back-EMF, so speed is `8.67/0.012 ≈ 722 rad/s`. The motor parameters are explicitly **estimated teaching values, not measurements**: [parameter definitions](/Users/elliot/physics-simulator/lessons/motor-torque-speed/motor.system.json:62).

**Why does adding load slow it down?** Initially, load torque exceeds motor torque, so the rotor decelerates. Lower speed reduces back-EMF, allowing more current and therefore more motor torque. It settles when motor torque balances the new load.

There is an important qualification to the quoted passage: during that transition, the full equations are:

```text
V = Ri + kₑω + L·di/dt
J·dω/dt = kₜi − opposing load torque
```

Consequently, current and speed cannot jump instantly, and transient points need not sit exactly on the steady torque–speed line. With the authored `L = 0.0005 H` and `J = 3×10⁻⁶ kg·m²`, the electrical time scale is `L/R = 0.25 ms`; the approximate mechanical time scale is `JR/(kₜkₑ) = 41.7 ms`. The [Rust implementation and model limits](/Users/elliot/physics-simulator/crates/sim-domain-bridges/src/elements.rs:227) include inductance but exclude friction, heating-dependent resistance, and magnetic saturation. That is why zero no-load current is an ideal-model result.

The current lesson still matches your quoted passage, and the system still declares revision 1. These numbers are analytical predictions; the supplied context contains no `model_context`, viewer status, or fresh run results to verify simulation behavior.
